entries.title: Network Security: App Transport Security Arbitrary Loads Allowed
entries.description: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads=true disables ATS globally; non-HTTPS connections are permitted.
entries.impact: The app may communicate with backends over plaintext HTTP; an on-path attacker can read or modify any unencrypted traffic, including authentication tokens.
entries.remediation_brief: Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads or scope to specific domains via NSExceptionDomains.

entries.title: Network Security: ATS Exception Allows HTTP for {dom}
entries.description: Per-domain NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads exception bypasses ATS for the listed domain.
entries.impact: Traffic to the excepted domain is plaintext and subject to interception. Acceptable only for legacy backends you control and have committed to migrating.
entries.remediation_brief: Migrate the backend to HTTPS and remove the exception.

entries.title: Attack Surface: Custom URL Scheme Registered: {sch}://
entries.description: Custom URL scheme allows any app on the device to invoke this app with arbitrary parameters.
entries.impact: If deep-link handlers don't validate parameters or enforce authentication, a malicious app could trigger sensitive actions (password change, in-app purchase, etc.). Verify each handler.
entries.remediation_brief: Validate every parameter; require re-authentication for sensitive actions; prefer Universal Links over custom schemes where possible.

entries.title: Build Configuration: get-task-allow Enabled (Debuggable Binary)
entries.description: The binary's entitlements set get-task-allow=true, allowing debuggers to attach.
entries.impact: An attacker on a jailbroken device can attach lldb to the running process and read memory, dump keychain items, or modify runtime behaviour. Should never ship in App Store builds.
entries.remediation_brief: Set get-task-allow=false in the production entitlements file before signing.

entries.title: Build Configuration: Wildcard Application-Identifier in Entitlements
entries.description: Wildcard provisioning profile (e.g. com.example.*) used in entitlements.
entries.impact: Keychain access groups and shared containers are scoped wider than intended; other apps signed with the same wildcard can read shared keychain entries.
entries.remediation_brief: Use specific bundle-identifier provisioning profiles in production.

entries.title: Information Disclosure: Potential hard-coded secret: {label}
entries.description: Pattern matching a known secret format (AWS access key, Google API key, private key, …) was found in the bundle.
entries.impact: Hard-coded secrets in client binaries are trivially recoverable by anyone with the IPA. If valid in production they grant the attacker the same privileges as the app, often including server-side actions the user is not authorised for.
entries.remediation_brief: Rotate the exposed secret; remove from the bundle; fetch via authenticated server call.

entries.title: Binary Security: NX (No-Execute) Bit Not Confirmed
entries.description: The iOS binary Mach-O header does not include the MH_NO_HEAP_EXECUTION flag, indicating that the NX (No eXecute) heap protection may not be enforced.
entries.impact: Without NX heap protection an attacker who achieves a heap overflow can place shellcode on the heap and execute it directly, simplifying exploitation of memory-corruption vulnerabilities.
entries.remediation_brief: Compile the binary with standard Xcode settings that enable NX and heap protection; avoid disabling MH_NO_HEAP_EXECUTION.

entries.title: Binary Security: PIE (Position Independent Executable) Not Enabled
entries.description: The iOS binary Mach-O header does not include the MH_PIE flag. Without PIE, Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) cannot randomize the binary's load address.
entries.impact: An attacker exploiting a memory-corruption bug can predict code and data addresses reliably, making ROP chains and return-to-libc attacks significantly easier. All App Store binaries are expected to be PIE.
entries.remediation_brief: Recompile the binary as a Position Independent Executable (PIE); in Xcode ensure 'Generate Position-Dependent Code' is set to NO.

entries.title: Binary Security: Stack Canary (Stack Protector) Missing
entries.description: The iOS binary does not import ___stack_chk_fail or ___stack_chk_guard symbols, indicating that stack smashing protection (-fstack-protector) is not compiled in.
entries.impact: Without stack canaries, a buffer overflow on the stack can silently overwrite the return address and redirect execution. Stack canaries detect such corruption before the function returns, making exploitation materially harder.
entries.remediation_brief: Compile with -fstack-protector-all (Xcode default for release builds); verify ___stack_chk_fail appears in the symbol table.

entries.title: Binary Security: ARC (Automatic Reference Counting) Not Enabled
entries.description: The iOS binary does not import _objc_release, indicating that Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) is not enabled for the Objective-C codebase.
entries.impact: Manual memory management without ARC is prone to use-after-free, double-free, and dangling-pointer vulnerabilities. An attacker who triggers such a bug can achieve arbitrary code execution.
entries.remediation_brief: Enable ARC for all Objective-C source files (Xcode: Objective-C Automatic Reference Counting = YES); migrate any manual retain/release code.

entries.title: Binary Security: RPATH Load Command Present in Binary
entries.description: The Mach-O binary contains one or more LC_RPATH load commands that define runtime library search paths.
entries.impact: While RPATH is commonly used for framework loading, a writable or user-controllable RPATH entry on a jailbroken device could allow dylib injection. Review paths to ensure none are attacker-writable.
entries.remediation_brief: Audit LC_RPATH entries; remove any that point to writable or non-standard paths; use @rpath/@executable_path relative references.

entries.title: Binary Security: Code Signature Missing or Invalid
entries.description: The codesign utility reports that the main binary lacks a valid code signature.
entries.impact: An unsigned binary cannot be verified for integrity or publisher identity. On a jailbroken device an attacker could replace or patch the binary without detection. Unsigned apps are rejected by the App Store.
entries.remediation_brief: Sign the binary with a valid Apple Developer certificate before distribution.

entries.title: Binary Security: Binary Not Encrypted (FairPlay DRM Absent)
entries.description: The LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO / LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO_64 load command shows cryptid=0, meaning the binary is not encrypted with Apple's FairPlay DRM.
entries.impact: An unencrypted binary can be directly disassembled and reverse-engineered without a decryption step. This lowers the bar for extracting proprietary algorithms, API keys, and business logic.
entries.remediation_brief: Distribute the app through the App Store (which applies FairPlay encryption automatically); for enterprise distribution consider additional code-obfuscation tools.

entries.title: Information Disclosure: Debug Symbols Not Stripped from Binary
entries.description: The nm utility reports that the binary still contains symbol names, indicating debug symbols have not been stripped for the release build.
entries.impact: Debug symbols reveal internal class names, method names, and data structures, significantly aiding reverse engineering. While not directly exploitable, they lower the cost of discovering vulnerabilities.
entries.remediation_brief: Enable Strip Linked Product and Strip Debug Symbols During Copy in Xcode release build settings; run 'strip' on the binary before packaging.

entries.title: Binary Security: Insecure C API Usage Detected
entries.description: The iOS binary imports potentially dangerous C standard library functions (e.g. strcpy, strcat, sprintf, gets, memcpy) that are known sources of buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
entries.impact: Use of unsafe C string and memory functions without bounds checking can lead to stack and heap buffer overflows. An attacker who controls the input to these functions can achieve arbitrary code execution.
entries.remediation_brief: Replace unsafe C functions with bounds-checked alternatives: strlcpy/strlcat instead of strcpy/strcat, snprintf instead of sprintf, fgets instead of gets, memcpy_s or explicit length checks.

entries.title: Information Disclosure: NSLog Usage Detected in Binary
entries.description: The iOS binary imports _NSLog, which writes to the system console log. Production builds should not log sensitive data.
entries.impact: NSLog output is readable by any app on a jailbroken device and by anyone with physical access via Xcode or Console.app. Sensitive data (tokens, passwords, PII) logged via NSLog is exposed to other processes and forensic extraction.
entries.remediation_brief: Remove or guard NSLog calls in release builds; use os_log with appropriate privacy levels or a logging framework that strips debug logs from production.

entries.title: Binary Security: malloc Used Without calloc (Uninitialized Memory Risk)
entries.description: The binary imports _malloc but does not import _calloc. malloc returns uninitialized memory, which can leak sensitive data if not explicitly zeroed.
entries.impact: Uninitialized heap memory may contain residual data from previous allocations (passwords, tokens, keys). If the application reads these bytes before writing, it may inadvertently process or expose stale secrets. Using calloc instead auto-zeros allocated memory.
entries.remediation_brief: Prefer calloc over malloc for security-sensitive allocations; alternatively memset allocated buffers to zero immediately after malloc.

entries.title: Framework Binary Weakness: {check}
entries.description: A bundled framework or dylib binary is missing a standard exploit mitigation (stack canary or ARC). The same protections required of the main binary apply to all embedded code.
entries.impact: A vulnerability in a bundled framework without stack canaries or ARC is as exploitable as one in the main binary. Third-party frameworks are a common attack surface because they are less frequently audited.
entries.remediation_brief: Rebuild or obtain updated versions of bundled frameworks compiled with -fstack-protector-all and ARC enabled; contact the framework vendor if source is unavailable.

entries.title: iOS Permission: {permission_key}
entries.description: The application's Info.plist declares a privacy-sensitive usage description key, requesting access to a protected resource (camera, microphone, location, contacts, etc.).
entries.impact: Each privacy permission grants the app access to sensitive user data. While individually justifiable, the combination of permissions defines the app's data reach. An attacker who compromises the app inherits all granted permissions.
entries.remediation_brief: Verify each permission is justified by the app's core functionality; remove any permissions not strictly necessary; request permissions just-in-time rather than at launch.

entries.title: iOS Permission: Excessive Permissions
entries.description: The application requests more than 6 sensitive iOS privacy permissions, indicating a broad data-access footprint that exceeds what most single-purpose apps require.
entries.impact: An app with excessive permissions exposes a wider attack surface: if compromised, the attacker gains access to camera, microphone, location, contacts, health data, and more simultaneously. Users and reviewers should question whether every permission is essential.
entries.remediation_brief: Audit all declared usage-description keys in Info.plist; remove permissions not essential to core functionality; apply the principle of least privilege.

entries.title: Application is debuggable
entries.description: android:debuggable=true allows attaching a debugger to the running app, enabling memory inspection, method interception, and data extraction.
entries.impact: An attacker on a rooted device or via ADB can attach a debugger (jdb, LLDB) to the running process, inspect heap memory, modify variables at runtime, bypass authentication checks, and extract encryption keys or credentials from memory.
entries.remediation_brief: Set android:debuggable=false in the AndroidManifest.xml for all release builds; use build variants to ensure debug flags never ship to production.

entries.title: Application allows backup
entries.description: android:allowBackup is true (or not explicitly set to false), allowing adb backup to extract application data including databases and shared preferences.
entries.impact: An attacker with physical access or ADB access can extract the entire app sandbox via 'adb backup', obtaining databases, SharedPreferences, cached credentials, session tokens, and other sensitive files without root access.
entries.remediation_brief: Set android:allowBackup=false in AndroidManifest.xml, or implement a BackupAgent that encrypts sensitive data before backup.

entries.title: Cleartext traffic allowed
entries.description: android:usesCleartextTraffic=true allows unencrypted HTTP connections globally from the application.
entries.impact: All network traffic from the app can be sent over plaintext HTTP. An on-path attacker (e.g. on public Wi-Fi) can intercept, read, and modify requests and responses including authentication credentials, session tokens, and personal data.
entries.remediation_brief: Set android:usesCleartextTraffic=false in AndroidManifest.xml; use a network security config to scope any necessary cleartext exceptions to specific domains.

entries.title: Exported {component_type} without permission: {name}
entries.description: An Android component (activity, service, receiver, or provider) is exported and accessible by any app without requiring a custom permission.
entries.impact: Any app on the device can invoke the exported component directly via an Intent. If the component handles sensitive operations (user data, transactions, internal APIs) without its own authentication, an attacker's app can abuse it to extract data or trigger privileged actions.
entries.remediation_brief: Set android:exported=false on components that do not need to be externally accessible; add a custom permission with android:protectionLevel='signature' to restrict access.

entries.title: Low minimum SDK version: API {version}
entries.description: The application's minSdkVersion targets an Android API level below 24 (Android 7.0), which lacks several modern security features.
entries.impact: Devices running older Android versions do not enforce network security config by default, lack file-based encryption, do not support scoped storage, and miss numerous security patches. The app's security posture is limited to the lowest supported platform.
entries.remediation_brief: Raise minSdkVersion to at least API 24 (Android 7.0) to inherit network security config, file-based encryption, and other platform security features.

entries.title: Excessive dangerous permissions ({count})
entries.description: The application requests more than 10 Android dangerous (runtime) permissions, indicating an overly broad data-access footprint.
entries.impact: Excessive permissions expand the attack surface: if the app is compromised, the attacker inherits access to camera, microphone, location, contacts, SMS, storage, and more. Users are less likely to scrutinize individual permission prompts when there are many.
entries.remediation_brief: Audit all dangerous permission requests; remove any not strictly required by core functionality; apply the principle of least privilege.

entries.title: Dangerous permission: {name}
entries.description: The app requests a specific Android dangerous (runtime) permission, classified by Android as granting access to sensitive user data or device capabilities.
entries.impact: Each dangerous permission grants access to a sensitive resource (camera, microphone, location, contacts, etc.). While individually justifiable, each adds to the app's data-access footprint and the potential impact if the app is compromised.
entries.remediation_brief: Verify the permission is justified by the app's core functionality; request it just-in-time rather than at launch; remove if not essential.

entries.title: Information Disclosure: Potential hard-coded secret: {label}
entries.description: Pattern matching a known secret format (AWS access key, Google API key, private key, JWT, etc.) was found in the APK bundle (DEX, smali, or resource files).
entries.impact: Hard-coded secrets in APKs are trivially recoverable via decompilation (jadx, apktool). If valid in production they grant the attacker the same privileges as the app, often including server-side API access, cloud resource manipulation, or payment processing.
entries.remediation_brief: Rotate the exposed secret immediately; remove from the APK; fetch credentials via an authenticated server call at runtime.

entries.title: Network Security Config: base config allows cleartext traffic
entries.description: The network_security_config.xml base-config element has cleartextTrafficPermitted='true', allowing unencrypted HTTP connections to all domains by default.
entries.impact: All HTTP traffic from the app is unencrypted. An on-path attacker can intercept, read, and modify every request and response, including credentials, session tokens, and personal data. This overrides Android's default HTTPS-only behaviour on API 28+.
entries.remediation_brief: Set cleartextTrafficPermitted='false' in the base-config; use domain-config exceptions only for domains that genuinely require HTTP and are on a migration path.

entries.title: Network Security Config: domain config trusts user-installed certificates
entries.description: A domain-config in network_security_config.xml includes a trust-anchors element with certificates src='user', causing the app to trust user-installed CA certificates for that domain.
entries.impact: An attacker who installs their own CA certificate on the device (via social engineering, MDM, or physical access) can perform a man-in-the-middle attack against the configured domain. All HTTPS traffic to that domain can be intercepted and decrypted.
entries.remediation_brief: Remove certificates src='user' from trust-anchors in production builds; trust only system CAs or pin specific certificates.

entries.title: Network Security Config: domain permits cleartext traffic
entries.description: A domain-config in network_security_config.xml permits cleartext traffic (cleartextTrafficPermitted='true') for a specific domain with includeSubdomains='true'.
entries.impact: HTTP traffic to the specified domain and all its subdomains is unencrypted and subject to interception. While scoped to a specific domain, any subdomain matching the pattern inherits the cleartext exception, broadening the exposure.
entries.remediation_brief: Migrate the domain to HTTPS and remove the cleartext exception; if HTTP is temporarily necessary, scope the domain-config to the narrowest domain without includeSubdomains.

entries.title: Dynamic: SSL pinning bypass — vulnerable (Android)
entries.description: Frida SSL pinning bypass succeeded on Android target, indicating the app does not implement certificate pinning or its implementation is bypassable.
entries.impact: An attacker can position a proxy between the app and its server to intercept, read, and modify all HTTPS traffic including authentication tokens and sensitive data.
entries.remediation_brief: Implement certificate pinning using TrustKit, OkHttp CertificatePinner, or network_security_config with pin-set.

entries.title: Dynamic: Root detection bypass — vulnerable (Android)
entries.description: Frida root detection bypass succeeded; the app does not adequately detect a rooted environment or its checks are easily bypassed.
entries.impact: An attacker on a rooted device can hook runtime methods, extract credentials from memory, bypass payment flows, and tamper with app logic without the app detecting the hostile environment.

mitre_attack.name: Modify OS Kernel or Boot Partition

entries.remediation_brief: Implement multi-layered root detection (SafetyNet/Play Integrity, file-based, property-based) with obfuscation.

entries.title: Dynamic: Data storage monitoring — insecure storage detected (Android)
entries.description: Frida data storage hooks captured SharedPreferences writes or SQLite queries containing potentially sensitive data.
entries.impact: Sensitive data stored in SharedPreferences or SQLite in plaintext can be extracted from a rooted device or from adb backup if allowBackup is true.
entries.remediation_brief: Encrypt sensitive data at rest using EncryptedSharedPreferences or SQLCipher; avoid storing secrets locally.

entries.title: Dynamic: Weak cryptographic API usage detected (Android)
entries.description: Frida crypto hooks observed the app using deprecated or weak cryptographic transforms (DES, ECB mode, MD5, SHA1 for integrity).
entries.impact: Weak cryptography can be broken by an attacker to decrypt stored data, forge tokens, or bypass integrity checks.
entries.remediation_brief: Replace weak algorithms with AES-256-GCM for encryption and SHA-256+ for hashing; avoid ECB mode.

entries.title: Dynamic: WebView security issue detected (Android)
entries.description: Frida WebView hooks detected WebView debug mode enabled or JavaScript enabled in a WebView that loads external content.
entries.impact: Debug-enabled WebViews allow Chrome DevTools attachment on rooted devices. JavaScript-enabled WebViews loading external content are susceptible to XSS and data exfiltration.
entries.remediation_brief: Disable setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled in production; restrict JavaScript to trusted content only.

entries.title: Dynamic: SSL pinning bypass — vulnerable (iOS)
entries.description: Frida SSL pinning bypass succeeded on iOS target via SSLSetSessionOption or NSURLSession hooks.
entries.impact: Same as Android: all HTTPS traffic can be intercepted, including tokens and PII.
entries.remediation_brief: Implement TrustKit or URLSessionDelegate-based certificate pinning.

entries.title: Dynamic: Jailbreak detection bypass — vulnerable (iOS)
entries.description: Frida jailbreak detection bypass succeeded; the app does not detect or adequately prevent running on a jailbroken device.
entries.impact: On a jailbroken device an attacker can hook Objective-C methods, dump the keychain, bypass payment logic, and modify runtime behaviour.
entries.remediation_brief: Implement multi-layered jailbreak detection (file-based, dylib injection, Cydia checks) with runtime integrity validation.

entries.title: Dynamic: Keychain monitoring — insecure keychain usage (iOS)
entries.description: Frida keychain hooks detected SecItemAdd/SecItemCopyMatching activity, indicating keychain usage that may store sensitive items with weak access controls.
entries.impact: Keychain items with kSecAttrAccessibleAlways or without access-group restrictions can be extracted by a jailbroken-device attacker or from an iTunes backup.
entries.remediation_brief: Use kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly for sensitive items; set access groups explicitly.

entries.title: Code Analysis: WebView JavaScript enabled
entries.description: The application calls WebSettings.setJavaScriptEnabled(true), enabling JavaScript execution inside a WebView.
entries.impact: If the WebView loads content from untrusted sources, an attacker can inject malicious JavaScript (XSS) to steal cookies, session tokens, or local storage data and relay it to an external server.
entries.remediation_brief: Disable JavaScript in WebViews that display untrusted content; validate and sanitize all data loaded via loadUrl/loadData.

entries.title: Code Analysis: WebView file access enabled
entries.description: The application calls WebSettings.setAllowFileAccess(true), allowing the WebView to read local files via file:// URIs.
entries.impact: Combined with JavaScript execution, an attacker exploiting an XSS vulnerability can read local app files (databases, SharedPreferences, cached credentials) via file:// and exfiltrate them.
entries.remediation_brief: Set setAllowFileAccess(false) unless file access is explicitly required; scope to specific paths if needed.

entries.title: Code Analysis: WebView universal file URL access
entries.description: The application calls WebSettings.setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true), allowing file:// pages to access content from any origin.
entries.impact: An attacker who can write a local file (e.g. via a download or cache poisoning) can load it in the WebView and use JavaScript to read content from any other origin, including the app's own sandbox files and HTTPS endpoints.
entries.remediation_brief: Set setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(false) (default since API 16); never enable for production builds.

entries.title: Code Analysis: JavaScript interface exposed
entries.description: The application calls WebView.addJavascriptInterface(), exposing a Java object to JavaScript running inside the WebView.
entries.impact: On API < 17, ALL public methods of the exposed object are callable from JavaScript, enabling arbitrary code execution via reflection. On API >= 17, only @JavascriptInterface methods are exposed, but bridge calls still execute with the app's full permissions.
entries.remediation_brief: Limit exposed methods; validate all input from JavaScript bridge calls; require minSdkVersion >= 17.

entries.title: Code Analysis: WebView debugging enabled
entries.description: The application enables WebView remote debugging via WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true).
entries.impact: On a rooted/USB-debuggable device, Chrome DevTools can connect to the WebView to inspect page content, execute arbitrary JavaScript, intercept network traffic, and extract sensitive data displayed in the WebView.
entries.remediation_brief: Disable setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled in release builds; guard with BuildConfig.DEBUG check.

entries.title: Code Analysis: Runtime.exec() command execution
entries.description: The application invokes java.lang.Runtime.exec() to execute a system command.
entries.impact: If user-controlled or externally influenced data reaches the command argument without sanitization, an attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands for execution with the app's UID and permissions.
entries.remediation_brief: Avoid Runtime.exec(); if required, use fixed command strings with no user input concatenation.

entries.title: Code Analysis: ProcessBuilder command execution
entries.description: The application uses java.lang.ProcessBuilder to execute system commands.
entries.impact: Same as Runtime.exec() — if attacker-controlled data influences the command or arguments, arbitrary command injection is possible.
entries.remediation_brief: Avoid ProcessBuilder; if required, use fixed command strings without user input.

entries.title: Code Analysis: Weak cryptographic algorithm
entries.description: The application uses a known-weak cryptographic algorithm or mode (ECB, DES, 3DES) via javax.crypto.Cipher.getInstance().
entries.impact: ECB mode leaks patterns in encrypted data; DES provides only 56-bit key strength. An attacker can exploit these weaknesses to decrypt stored secrets, authentication tokens, or user data.
entries.remediation_brief: Use AES-256 with GCM or CBC mode and proper IV management; avoid ECB mode and DES/3DES entirely.

entries.title: Code Analysis: SecureRandom seeded predictably
entries.description: The application calls SecureRandom.setSeed(), which on certain Android versions can replace OS entropy with a developer-supplied (possibly predictable) seed.
entries.impact: A predictable random number generator can allow an attacker to predict session tokens, encryption keys, nonces, or OTPs, leading to authentication bypass or data decryption.
entries.remediation_brief: Do not call setSeed(); let the default constructor provide OS entropy. Use new SecureRandom() directly.

entries.title: Code Analysis: Direct SQL query construction
entries.description: The application constructs SQL queries directly via SQLiteDatabase.rawQuery() or execSQL() with a String argument rather than parameterized queries.
entries.impact: If user input is concatenated into the SQL string, an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete database contents, bypassing authentication or exfiltrating stored secrets.
entries.remediation_brief: Use parameterized queries (selectionArgs in rawQuery, bindArgs in execSQL) instead of string concatenation.

entries.title: Code Analysis: World-readable/writable file mode
entries.description: The application creates files with MODE_WORLD_READABLE or MODE_WORLD_WRITABLE, making them accessible to all apps on the device.
entries.impact: Any app on the device can read (or write) the file. If the file contains credentials, tokens, or personal data, an attacker's app can silently exfiltrate it. Writable files allow data injection or tampering.
entries.remediation_brief: Use MODE_PRIVATE for all file creation; share data between apps via ContentProviders with proper permissions.

entries.title: Code Analysis: Hostname verifier bypass
entries.description: The application overrides or disables SSL hostname verification using ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER or a custom HostnameVerifier that accepts all hostnames.
entries.impact: An attacker with a valid certificate for ANY domain can perform a man-in-the-middle attack against the app's HTTPS connections. All traffic can be intercepted even though TLS is nominally in use.
entries.remediation_brief: Use the default HostnameVerifier; do not override with ALLOW_ALL or a permissive custom verifier.

entries.title: Code Analysis: Data written to clipboard
entries.description: The application writes data to the system clipboard via ClipboardManager.setPrimaryClip().
entries.impact: On Android < 10 (API 29), any app can read the clipboard at any time without user interaction. If the app copies passwords, tokens, or PII, a malicious background app can harvest them silently.
entries.remediation_brief: Avoid writing sensitive data to the clipboard; if necessary, clear it after a short timeout.

entries.title: Code Analysis: Excessive logging
entries.description: The application contains an excessive number of android.util.Log calls (debug, verbose, info, error), indicating verbose logging in the release build.
entries.impact: Log output is written to logcat, which on rooted devices or via ADB is readable by any process. Sensitive data (tokens, credentials, PII, internal URLs, error details) logged at any level can be captured by an attacker.
entries.remediation_brief: Remove or guard verbose/debug logging in release builds; use ProGuard/R8 rules to strip Log.d/v/i calls.

entries.title: Third-party tracker SDK detected: {tracker_name}
entries.description: The APK bundles a known third-party tracker or analytics SDK, identified by its package path in the DEX/smali code.
entries.impact: Tracker SDKs collect user behaviour data (screen views, events, device identifiers) and transmit it to external servers. This may violate user privacy expectations and regulatory requirements (GDPR, CCPA) if consent is not properly obtained.
entries.remediation_brief: Audit tracker SDKs for data collection scope; ensure user consent is obtained; provide opt-out mechanisms.

entries.title: Excessive third-party trackers detected ({count})
entries.description: The APK bundles more than 5 distinct third-party tracker or analytics SDKs.
entries.impact: Each tracker SDK collects and transmits user data independently, compounding privacy exposure. Multiple trackers increase the attack surface (each is a dependency that may have vulnerabilities) and the volume of data leaving the device.
entries.remediation_brief: Review and remove unnecessary tracker SDKs; consolidate analytics to the fewest providers that meet business requirements.

entries.title: Protection: Anti-debug mechanism detected
entries.description: The app implements anti-debugging checks (e.g. isDebuggerConnected(), ptrace self-trace) to detect runtime analysis.
entries.impact: Anti-debug mechanisms are a positive security control that makes dynamic analysis harder for attackers. Their presence indicates the developer has invested in runtime integrity protection.
entries.remediation_brief: No remediation needed — this is a positive security control. Consider strengthening with multi-layered detection.

entries.title: Protection: Anti-emulator detection found
entries.description: The app checks for emulator/virtual-machine indicators (Build.FINGERPRINT, Build.MODEL, goldfish, generic) to detect analysis environments.
entries.impact: Anti-emulator checks are a positive security control that prevents automated analysis in emulators. Their presence indicates the developer is protecting against sandbox-based malware analysis or dynamic testing.
entries.remediation_brief: No remediation needed — this is a positive security control.

entries.title: Protection: Packer/obfuscator detected: {name}
entries.description: The APK is protected by a code packer or obfuscator (e.g. DexGuard, Bangcle, ProGuard/R8, Tencent, Secneo).
entries.impact: Packers and obfuscators make reverse engineering harder and slow down attackers. Their presence is a positive indicator of investment in intellectual property protection and anti-tampering.
entries.remediation_brief: No remediation needed — this is a positive security control.

entries.title: Protection: No code obfuscation detected
entries.description: The APK does not appear to use code obfuscation (no ProGuard/R8 mapping, no known packer signatures, readable class and method names).
entries.impact: Without obfuscation, an attacker can decompile the APK (via jadx or apktool) and read the source code almost as clearly as the original, making it trivial to discover business logic, API endpoints, hardcoded secrets, and vulnerability patterns.
entries.remediation_brief: Enable ProGuard/R8 in the release build configuration; consider DexGuard or similar commercial obfuscators for sensitive applications.

entries.title: Firebase Realtime Database URL exposed
entries.description: A Firebase Realtime Database URL (*.firebaseio.com) was found in the APK. If database security rules are misconfigured, the database may be publicly readable or writable.
entries.impact: An attacker can attempt to access the Firebase database directly from a browser or tool. If rules allow unauthenticated reads, all stored data (user records, messages, configurations) is exposed. If writes are allowed, the attacker can inject or delete data.
entries.remediation_brief: Enforce Firebase Security Rules requiring authentication for all reads and writes; use role-based access control.

entries.title: Firebase Storage URL exposed
entries.description: A Firebase Cloud Storage URL (firebasestorage.googleapis.com) was found in the APK.
entries.impact: If storage security rules are misconfigured, an attacker can list, download, or upload files to the bucket without authentication, potentially accessing user-uploaded content or injecting malicious files.
entries.remediation_brief: Enforce Firebase Storage security rules requiring authentication; restrict file types and sizes; use per-user storage paths.

entries.title: Firebase configuration file (google-services.json) present
entries.description: The APK contains a google-services.json (or GoogleService-Info.plist) file with Firebase project configuration, including project ID, API key, and storage bucket.
entries.impact: While the API key alone cannot authenticate, the configuration reveals the Firebase project ID and bucket names, enabling targeted probing of database rules and storage permissions.
entries.remediation_brief: Ensure Firebase security rules are properly configured; restrict API key usage via Google Cloud Console.

entries.title: Firebase Remote Config usage detected
entries.description: The APK references Firebase Remote Config classes, indicating the app fetches configuration values from Firebase at runtime.
entries.impact: Remote Config values can influence app behaviour. If the Firebase project is compromised, an attacker could modify remote config to change app behaviour, redirect traffic, or enable hidden features.
entries.remediation_brief: Validate remote config values on the client before acting on them; use Firebase App Check to restrict access.

entries.title: APK uses only JAR signing (v1) — Janus vulnerability
entries.description: The APK is signed only with the v1 (JAR) scheme and lacks v2/v3 APK Signature Scheme protection, making it vulnerable to the Janus vulnerability (CVE-2017-13156).
entries.impact: An attacker can prepend a DEX file to a v1-only-signed APK. Android's installer verifies v1 (which only checks the ZIP entries) while the runtime loads the prepended DEX. This allows code injection into a legitimately signed app without breaking the signature.

mitre_attack.name: Modify OS Kernel or Boot Partition

entries.remediation_brief: Enable APK Signature Scheme v2 (and v3 if targeting API 28+) in your build configuration; both v1+v2 should be enabled for backward compatibility.

entries.title: APK certificate uses weak signing algorithm
entries.description: The APK signing certificate uses a weak hash algorithm (SHA1withRSA, MD5withRSA) that is vulnerable to collision attacks.
entries.impact: A weak signing hash allows an attacker to potentially generate a second certificate with the same hash, enabling signature forgery. While practical collision attacks against SHA-1 have been demonstrated, exploiting this in APK signing is complex but feasible for a resourced attacker.
entries.remediation_brief: Re-sign the APK with a certificate using SHA256withRSA or SHA384withRSA.

entries.title: APK signing certificate expired or expiring soon
entries.description: The APK signing certificate has expired or will expire within 90 days.
entries.impact: An expired certificate prevents app updates from being installed through the Play Store or sideloading, as Android requires consistent signing across versions. The developer may be forced to issue a new signing identity, breaking update paths for existing users.
entries.remediation_brief: Generate a new signing certificate with a long validity period (25+ years is standard for Android); use Play App Signing for key management.

entries.title: APK signed with debug certificate
entries.description: The APK is signed with an Android debug certificate (CN=Android Debug, typically from ~/.android/debug.keystore), which is a default keystore shared across developer machines.
entries.impact: The debug keystore password is publicly known ("android"). Any developer can sign an app with the same debug key and produce a matching package signature. This allows an attacker to create a malicious update that Android's installer accepts as legitimate.
entries.remediation_brief: Sign release builds with a dedicated release keystore; never distribute debug-signed APKs outside development.

entries.title: APK signing information
entries.description: Summary of the APK signing certificate details including Common Name, organization, validity period, key algorithm, and which APK Signature Scheme versions are present.
entries.impact: Informational. The signing certificate details are used to evaluate the overall signing posture of the application.
entries.remediation_brief: Review certificate details for appropriate key length (RSA 2048+), algorithm (SHA256+), and validity period.

entries.title: Browsable activity with deep link: {activity_name}
entries.description: An activity declares an intent filter with the BROWSABLE category, registering a deep link scheme (custom scheme:// or https:// App Link) that can be invoked from a browser or another app.
entries.impact: Deep links allow external invocation of specific app screens. If the receiving activity does not validate parameters, an attacker can craft a malicious link that triggers unintended actions (account linking, data display, state changes) when the user clicks it.
entries.remediation_brief: Validate all deep link parameters; require re-authentication for sensitive actions; prefer App Links (verified HTTPS) over custom schemes.

entries.title: Unprotected browsable activity: {activity_name}
entries.description: A browsable activity is exported without a custom permission, meaning any app or web page can invoke it with arbitrary parameters via its deep link.
entries.impact: An attacker can craft a link (in a phishing email, web page, or malicious app) that opens the unprotected activity with attacker-controlled parameters. This can be used to bypass navigation flows, inject data into forms, or trigger privileged operations without user consent.
entries.remediation_brief: Validate all incoming Intent data; require user confirmation for sensitive actions; use App Links with digital asset verification.

entries.title: Behaviour: SMS sending capability
entries.description: The app uses SmsManager API (sendTextMessage/sendMultipartTextMessage) and declares the SEND_SMS permission, giving it the ability to send SMS messages programmatically.
entries.impact: If the app is compromised, the SMS capability can be used to send premium-rate messages (billing fraud), exfiltrate data via SMS, or participate in SMS-based social engineering campaigns — all transparent to the user.
entries.remediation_brief: Verify SMS capability is justified by core functionality; remove SEND_SMS permission if not essential.

entries.title: Behaviour: Phone call initiation capability
entries.description: The app uses Intent.ACTION_CALL or TelecomManager APIs with the CALL_PHONE permission, allowing it to initiate phone calls without user interaction via the dialer.
entries.impact: A compromised app with direct call capability can silently dial premium-rate numbers (billing fraud) or be used for harassment. ACTION_CALL bypasses the dialer UI entirely.
entries.remediation_brief: Use ACTION_DIAL instead of ACTION_CALL to require user confirmation; remove CALL_PHONE permission if not essential.

entries.title: Behaviour: Contact access capability
entries.description: The app accesses the contacts database (ContactsContract provider) with READ_CONTACTS or WRITE_CONTACTS permission.
entries.impact: Contact data is highly sensitive PII. A compromised app with contacts access can exfiltrate the user's entire address book (names, phone numbers, emails, photos), which is a common technique used by spyware and social engineering platforms.
entries.remediation_brief: Verify contacts access is justified; remove READ_CONTACTS/WRITE_CONTACTS if not essential; minimize data read.

entries.title: Behaviour: Location tracking capability
entries.description: The app actively tracks the user's location via requestLocationUpdates, getLastKnownLocation, or FusedLocationProviderClient with fine or coarse location permissions.
entries.impact: Location data reveals the user's physical movements, home and work addresses, and daily patterns. A compromised app with location tracking can surveil the user in real time or build a historical location profile.
entries.remediation_brief: Verify location tracking is justified; use coarse location when fine is not needed; minimize tracking duration; remove if not essential.

entries.title: Behaviour: Camera capture capability
entries.description: The app accesses the device camera via Camera API, CameraManager, or ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE with the CAMERA permission.
entries.impact: A compromised app with camera access can silently capture photos or video of the user's surroundings, constituting covert surveillance. This is a high-sensitivity permission often targeted by spyware.
entries.remediation_brief: Verify camera access is justified; remove CAMERA permission if not essential; use ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE for one-shot photos.

entries.title: Behaviour: Audio recording capability
entries.description: The app uses MediaRecorder, AudioRecord, or similar APIs with the RECORD_AUDIO permission, giving it the ability to capture audio from the device microphone.
entries.impact: A compromised app with audio recording capability can silently record conversations, meetings, and ambient audio, constituting covert surveillance. This is among the most sensitive permissions on mobile devices.
entries.remediation_brief: Verify audio recording is justified; remove RECORD_AUDIO permission if not essential; consider push-to-talk patterns to limit recording duration.

entries.title: Cleartext HTTP Traffic to {host}
entries.description: The mobile application sends HTTP (unencrypted) traffic to a backend host. All request and response data traverses the network in plaintext.
entries.impact: An on-path attacker (shared Wi-Fi, compromised router, ISP-level) can read every byte of the communication — authentication tokens, personal data, API responses — and silently modify it in transit.
entries.remediation_brief: Enforce HTTPS for all network communications. Implement HSTS on the server side and certificate pinning in the application.

entries.title: Sensitive Data in URL ({pattern})
entries.description: The request URL contains sensitive data (password, token, SSN, email, credit card, or API key) in its query parameters.
entries.impact: URL query parameters are recorded in server access logs, browser history, proxy caches, HTTP referer headers, and analytics platforms. Credentials or PII in URLs are persistently exposed across multiple systems beyond the intended recipient.
entries.owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
entries.remediation_brief: Move sensitive data from URL query parameters to request headers (e.g. Authorization) or POST request bodies. Enforce HTTPS for all endpoints.

entries.title: Sensitive Data in {src} Body ({pattern})
entries.description: The request or response body contains sensitive data such as SSNs, credit card numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, or plaintext passwords.
entries.impact: Sensitive PII or credentials transmitted in API bodies may be logged, cached, or stored by intermediary systems. If the connection is intercepted, the data is immediately exploitable for identity theft or account takeover.
entries.owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
entries.remediation_brief: Minimize sensitive data in API requests and responses. Use tokenization for PII, field-level encryption for stored credentials, and ensure HTTPS is enforced.

entries.title: {header}: {host}
entries.description: The server response is missing a security header (Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, or X-Frame-Options).
entries.impact: Missing HSTS allows protocol-downgrade attacks; missing CSP permits XSS payload execution in WebViews; missing X-Content-Type-Options enables MIME-sniffing attacks; missing X-Frame-Options allows clickjacking.
entries.remediation_brief: Configure the web server to include the missing security header in all responses. Enable HSTS with a minimum max-age of 31536000.

entries.title: API Key/Token in Traffic ({key_type}): {host}
entries.description: A recognizable API key or token pattern (AWS access key, Google API key, Firebase key, GitHub token, Slack token, Stripe key, Twilio key, or Bearer token) was detected in the intercepted traffic.
entries.impact: Exposed API keys can be extracted by any attacker with network access and used to access cloud resources, make API calls, or escalate privileges in the associated service — often without rate-limiting or audit trail that points back to the attacker.
entries.remediation_brief: Rotate the exposed key immediately. Replace long-lived API keys with short-lived, scoped tokens (e.g. OAuth2 client credentials). Never embed keys in client-side applications.

entries.title: Insecure Cookie: {name} on {host}
entries.description: A Set-Cookie response header is missing one or more of the Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite flags.
entries.impact: A cookie without the Secure flag is transmitted over HTTP and can be intercepted. Without HttpOnly, JavaScript (including XSS payloads in WebViews) can read it. Without SameSite, the cookie is sent on cross-origin requests enabling CSRF.
entries.remediation_brief: Add the Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Strict (or Lax) flags to all session and sensitive cookies.

entries.title: TLS Certificate Issue: {host}
entries.description: The mitmproxy connection recorded a TLS error for the host, such as a self-signed certificate, expired certificate, or hostname mismatch.
entries.impact: Certificate errors indicate the application may accept invalid certificates, making it vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. An attacker on the network path can present their own certificate and intercept all encrypted traffic.
entries.remediation_brief: Use valid certificates from a trusted Certificate Authority. Implement certificate pinning in the mobile application to reject unexpected certificates.

entries.title: Third-Party Data Leakage: {tracker}
entries.description: The application sends data to a known third-party analytics or advertising SDK (e.g. Google Analytics, Facebook SDK, Adjust, AppsFlyer, Crashlytics). The transmitted data may include device identifiers, location data, or user identifiers.
entries.impact: Third-party SDKs transmit user data to external servers outside the application's control. This creates regulatory exposure (GDPR, CCPA), increases the attack surface via additional data stores, and may violate user privacy expectations if not disclosed.
entries.remediation_brief: Review all data sent to third-party analytics and advertising SDKs. Minimize PII transmission, anonymize device and user identifiers, and disclose all third-party data sharing in the privacy policy.

entries.title: Unencrypted Authentication: {host}
aliases: Credentials in URL on Auth Endpoint
entries.description: An authentication-related request (login, signin, token, OAuth endpoint) was sent over plaintext HTTP, or credentials were found in the URL of an authentication endpoint.
entries.impact: User credentials (username, password, session token) are transmitted in cleartext and visible to any network observer. An attacker can capture credentials for account takeover, or replay captured tokens to hijack active sessions.
entries.remediation_brief: All authentication endpoints MUST use HTTPS. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Implement HSTS. Send credentials in the request body, never in URL parameters.

entries.title: Deprecated TLS Version ({version}): {host}
entries.description: The connection to the host was negotiated using a deprecated TLS version (TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, SSLv2, or SSLv3) that has known cryptographic vulnerabilities.
entries.impact: Deprecated TLS versions are vulnerable to BEAST, POODLE, and other protocol-downgrade attacks that allow an attacker to decrypt traffic. Major browsers and compliance frameworks (PCI DSS) have deprecated these versions.
entries.remediation_brief: Configure the server to support TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 only. Disable TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, SSLv2, and SSLv3.
